title: iPhone Duo, One Month Later: I’m Not Ready to End the Love Affair
snippet: After making Apple’s foldable my daily companion, I’ve made peace with some shortcomings while resigning myself to others. Mostly, though, there’s been a lot to admire.
fullText:
One month after getting the iPhone Duo, I’ve stuck to my commitment to keep using it even after publishing my review. Well, mostly.

Apple’s debut foldable has proven to be a practical everyday device, whether I’m streaming movies, texting or getting work done. I’ve grown so accustomed to using it that I sometimes forget how much attention it draws when I pull it out of my pocket, especially given its limited availability and lengthy preorder windows – not to mention its sky-high $1,999 starting price.

Still, there have been times when I’ve reached for the iPhone 18 Pro Max instead for its more advanced camera system, as well as its familiar, straightforward design. The Duo’s cameras pull their weight with casual photography, but while filming social content at F1’s US Grand Prix and chatting with filmmakers at an SFFilm screening, I couldn’t resist going for the best cameras at my disposal on the Pro Max. There are times a conventional slab phone just does the trick – without all the frills and novelty of a folding one. 

		

			

That hasn’t stopped me from keeping the Duo as my primary device. It’s an enjoyable phone to use, with its compact, palm-sized build and spacious inner display. Plus, as CNET’s ongoing folding test demonstrates, it has a durable build that ensures I can fold and unfold it to my heart’s content.

And if I’m being honest, I kind of love how much of a statement piece it’s become. 

Why I’m still using the iPhone Duo

The Duo’s versatility has really shown its appeal the more I live with it. I find myself using the 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display pretty equally, demonstrating the practicality of each. 

When I’m on the move, the cover screen suffices for sending texts, responding to emails and checking notifications. Lounging around at home, I’m more inclined to use the larger inner display to endlessly scroll through Instagram or binge YouTube videos. 

The matte inner display remains one of my favorite elements. It reduces the appearance of the crease as well as glare, making it easier to see content even outdoors. Yes, the coating can dim the vibrant colors in images and videos, even with the screen’s 3,000-nit peak brightness, and smudges become prominent. But I can live with both of those drawbacks, and a microfiber cloth fixes the latter. 

Apple’s phone-tablet hybrid came in clutch when I was on a recent flight and didn’t want to pull out my laptop. Instead, I used the Duo’s split-screen mode to place the Notes app on one half of the screen and an informational video on the other so I could quickly jot down the main points. The Duo has also become my gym buddy; I prop it open on the treadmill so I can watch Magpie Murders on a tablet-like display, then fold it up and toss it in my pocket when I’m done. 

Apple Pencil support levels up the experience 

Apple Pencil support really helps the Duo feel like a mini iPad, and the matte coating on the inner display adds a satisfying resistance that more closely emulates the feel of writing on paper than a glossy surface. It gives jotting down notes, highlighting book passages and marking up documents a more tactile feel. I’m not much of a doodler, but I imagine that’s fun, too. 

The Apple Pencil can magnetically attach to the outer surface of the hinge, though it definitely sticks out, so there’s not really a practical, secure way to carry it around with the Duo (at least not that Apple has shared, but case-makers are sure to cook up a solution). I’m glad the stylus also works on the Duo’s cover screen, though the smaller size and glossy display make that experience slightly less satisfying. 

More apps are being optimized

The number of apps optimized for the Duo at launch was relatively small, but it’s steadily increased. I gasped aloud on the train platform one morning while sending an email, realizing Gmail had finally been adapted for the Duo. It’s refreshing to see apps that feel intentional and fill the screen, rather than being awkwardly letterboxed.

Apple said in early November that more than 100,000 apps built for the iPhone Duo were live in the App Store. A week later, that number ballooned to over 200,000 apps. So despite a rather slow start, virtually all apps I regularly use now work seamlessly on Apple’s foldable. 

One of my favorite apps on the Duo is Instagram’s Edits. When holding the phone open in landscape orientation, I can view the video timeline and make edits on the right side of the screen while seeing a preview of the video on the left. Rotated to portrait orientation, the layout resembles the interface on a traditional smartphone, but on a larger scale, which is helpful especially for making smaller tweaks.

It’s great to see more apps that don’t just expand to the larger screen, but make meaningful use of the Duo’s design. 

Battery life has been solid

As I found during my review, the Duo’s battery life has been pretty good. It consistently lasts through the day, even as I hop between displays. I usually charge my phone at night, but even if I don’t, I know I’ll have some remaining battery in the morning.

For instance, one day I started at 6:30 a.m. with a full battery. After my usual routine of checking emails, texting, scrolling through social media and browsing YouTube throughout the day, my battery was at 55% by 9:12 p.m. The next morning, I woke up with 48% battery, and that charge lasted through a similar routine, along with phone calls, texting and music and video streaming, before the battery finally died at 7:30 p.m.

The Duo has yet to give me a reason to stress about its battery life. 

The camera is good enough

I will acknowledge I’m a tad pretentious when it comes to smartphone cameras. But if I’m documenting an event or photographing my fancy tea sets, I want the best cameras I can get. Unlike the Duo, iPhone 18 Pro models have a telephoto camera, more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors. 

Most of the time, the Duo’s 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras do the trick just fine. Colors are vivid, details are sharp and images are bright. Videos look good, too, though the 18 Pro Max does a noticeably better job with nighttime footage, which can look more muddy on the Duo. Digital video on the Duo also tops out at 6x, versus 24x on the Pros. Most of the time, though, I’m quite content with what I capture with the Duo’s cameras.

As I noted in my review, the under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen isn’t great, but I never really take selfies using that camera. It feels much more natural to use the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen, which serves up sharp photos every time. 

The cover screen selfie camera plays a critical role in an update that makes using the Duo even more seamless. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera. 

In the absence of Face ID, which I have felt rather painfully, this has been a solid workaround, even if it’s not as secure as Apple’s biometric facial recognition and authentication system. You’ll still need to use Touch ID or a passcode when using Apple Pay or accessing passwords, and to unlock the phone after leaving it alone for around 45 minutes. But a win is a win. (You can also unlock the Duo using an Apple Watch, but I don’t have one.)

		

			

I love the novelty 

I’ll admit I still feel a little bashful when pulling out the Duo because of how much attention it drums up, despite being far from the first foldable phone. But its limited availability and hype paired with the unique design make it eye-catching, for better or worse. Using the Duo has led to some fun conversations, whether it’s with a sales associate as I pay for a pastry or with Project Hail Mary directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, who spotted the phone in my hand during an interview and geeked out over it. That’s been a fun side effect of using Apple’s first foldable in my everyday life.

I’ve been living dangerously without a case; I don’t want anything to detract from the phone’s sleek feel. This is one of those “do as I say, not as I do” moments, as I’d recommend slapping a case on a phone that costs nearly $2,000. I did put a tempered glass screen protector on the cover display to guard against scratches. I can feel its edge against the otherwise flush surface of the phone when I hold it open, but aesthetic sacrifices must be made.

What I still don’t love about the iPhone Duo

The Duo isn’t perfect, even if I love using this phone. After holding Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo can feel slightly chunky. The Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when open and 9.7mm when closed. Meanwhile, the Duo is 5.2mm thick when open and 11.3mm when closed. It’s not a huge difference, but it makes me look forward to Apple hopefully slimming down the second-generation version, if and when it comes. 

The Duo is also slightly heavier than the Z Fold 8, weighing 254 grams (compared to 201 grams for Samsung’s foldable). I’m always surprised when people remark how heavy the Duo is, but I think the reason I don’t share that sentiment is that I’m accustomed to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which weighs 249 grams. 

When the Duo is open in landscape orientation, I’m glad there’s an option to split the keyboard so it’s easier to type across the wider expanse, but I wish the swipe functionality worked in that configuration, too. It’s a little thing that would make a noticeable difference for those of us who rely heavily on swipe-to-text. 

One drawback of the Duo’s compact design is that some existing MagSafe wallets and other accessories won’t stick to the back without awkwardly jutting out. So you might have to invest in some new accessories specifically designed for the Duo. 

Until the recent addition of face unlock, the Duo’s biggest drawback was the lack of Face ID. It’s a feature I’d expect on such a premium device, especially given that even the budget-focused iPhone 17E supports it. 

Touch ID works reliably on the Duo, but it’s slow compared to fingerprint unlock on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which also supports facial recognition). And while the new face unlock capability on the Duo isn’t an exact replacement for Face ID, which is more secure, it helps make accessing the phone’s contents more convenient and in line with the Duo’s modern aesthetics. 

Will I keep using the Duo?

I’ve finished my homework: My review is done, and now, so is this one-month follow-up. What’s next?

I’m not sure I’m ready to throw in the towel on Apple’s foldable just yet. The novelty of the iPhone Duo hasn’t worn off, and I’ve become quite used to my passport-size companion. It does just about everything I need, despite some slight imperfections, and it’s fun to use. It’s also amusing to see how people react when they see it in my hand.

So for now, it looks like the Duo will remain my daily driver. Whether the honeymoon phase eventually wears off remains to be seen, but I’m not in any hurry to end this love affair.

title: iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3
snippet: iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

#1: Face unlock

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple: 

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

#2: Reachability

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

#3: Automatically lock when closed

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Bonus: Keyboard updates

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

title: iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates
snippet: Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing. more…
fullText:
Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 suppliers planning for March launch, per report

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Kim Yeong-ho, writing at ETNews:

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

snippet: Apple is coming up to the end of its first year as the exclusive broadcaster of Formula 1 in the United States, with the deal set to continue through 2031. So far, it seems to be going well for all parties involved. In a sign of that relationship strengthening, the company announced it is expanding its racing coverage, with the all-female F1 Academy series joining the Apple TV platform next year. more…
fullText:
Apple is coming up to the end of its first year as the exclusive broadcaster of Formula 1 in the United States, with the deal set to continue through 2031. So far, it seems to be going well for all parties involved. 

In a sign of that relationship strengthening, the company announced it is expanding its racing coverage, with the all-female F1 Academy series joining the Apple TV platform next year. 

The F1 Academy season starts on March 19, 2027. And with this news, you’ll be able to watch it through the Apple TV app with an Apple TV subscription, joining the Formula 1 coverage. The schedule runs across seven races through November. 

Apple TV will feature full coverage of Academy qualifying and race sessions.

Since its inception in 2023, the F1 Academy series helps bring promote female talent in a sport that is currently dominated by male drivers.

title: The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone
snippet: VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone. more…
fullText:
VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with. 

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

	

VWFNDR explains:

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:

B+W
NIHON
NATURAL

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

VWFNDR + MBL on iPhone

Airfly Drive works with most cars that have factory-wired CarPlay, according to Twelve South. This covers more than 75 makes and model years back to 2014. Works with the car’s existing display, buttons, and steering-wheel controls.

Ongoing compatibility updates.

Wireless CarPlay is significantly more seamless than wired CarPlay, especially for those shorter trips around town. It’s a great quality-of-life update for your CarPlay experience.

title: OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons
snippet: Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro. The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited … more…
fullText:
Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

	

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

OLED iMac may be delayed or abandoned

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision. 

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be launched in around 2029.

title: Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro
snippet: The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead? more…
fullText:
The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

The answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

Ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

The same issue cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

Portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

title: Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)
snippet: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked. more…
fullText:
Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Jensen Huang responds to calls for him to return as CEO, says he would ‘be honored to answer these calls’

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

Here’s what Huang said:

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

	

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

title: One UI 9.5 Beta is out now for these Galaxy devices – how to install it
snippet: Samsung’s beta train has officially left the station, so to speak. One UI 9.5 is starting to roll out to these devices, and with it, some major changes to its Galaxy phones. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s beta train has officially left the station, so to speak. One UI 9.5 is starting to roll out to these devices, and with it, some major changes to its Galaxy phones.

One UI 9.5 Beta is an ‘early look’

There are a couple of reasons the One UI 9.5 beta packs a substantial punch on your Galaxy S26. For one, it’s a halfway mark between Android versions where more useful features can be implemented. Samsung started this trend of releasing the next half-step up in One UI versions with its standard flagships. That’s why, when the Galaxy S27 becomes official, it will launch with One UI 9.5 preloaded.

Samsung details some of the key changes we’ll see in the One UI 9.5 beta, like a new journaling app and better video/camera controls.

Enhanced Pro and Pro Video

	

Mindful note

Medications

Reminders and tracking

Floating shortcuts

Keep essential controls within reach

Improved hearing aid controls

App Lock

Secures individual apps for safer everyday use

Which devices get One UI 9.5 Beta?

It might be because the Galaxy S27 is the first device slated for the stable One UI 9.5 launch, but the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S26 Plus, and Galaxy S26 Ultra are the only devices that can access the beta update. The list doesn’t include the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Fold 8 Ultra, even though they’ve become some of the best devices Samsung has to offer.

Samsung also puts limitations on regions, noting the program will only be open in Germany, India, Korea, Poland, the UK, and the US. Users on other devices outside of those regions won’t be able to download the beta.

That isn’t to say they’re locked out forever. Samsung will very likely expand the beta program before the Galaxy S27 launch, meaning more devices will get access and in wider areas.

How to install the One UI 9.5 beta update

On your Galaxy S26, S26 Plus, or S26 Ultra, you’ll need to sign up for the One UI beta program once more. This is an entirely new beta program, and it doesn’t look like participants carry over from the One UI 9 beta.

Head over to the Samsung Members app on your Galaxy phone.

Scroll down and tap the card in the Beta program section.

Tap One UI 9.5 Beta and hit Join.

Tap again and hit Check for software update.

Alternatively, check your settings.

Update if available.

Once you finish that process, you should be all set with One UI 9.5 beta.

Once again, since it’s early access, you shouldn’t expect things to be perfect. If you find the experience is awful, you can always revert back.

The full One UI 9.5 Beta changelog

Samsung published the full changelog alongside its OTA update, as outlined below.

One UI 9.5 Beta

Camera

Improved camera controls and zoom bar

Quick controls are now laid out on one screen, so every option is visible without scrolling. The layout of the bottom shutter area has also been improved, providing a cleaner and simpler look.

Enhanced Pro and Pro video modes

You can now create custom buttons and presets, see lens and zoom levels as focal length, fine-tune manual sliders, and monitor your shot with an improved histogram and audio meter.

Lock screen personalization

Live effect for wallpapers

Add depth to your Lock screen wallpaper. As you tilt your device, elements in the image shift at different depths.

More customizable Lock screen clock

You can choose how long the clock with seconds appears on your Lock screen. Choose a timeout of 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, or 10 minutes from the settings in the upper-right corner.

Sports animations in Now bar

Animation effects are now available for more sports. Celebrate your favorite team’s goals and victories with special visual effects. You can download these effects in Now bar settings.

Digital Wellbeing

Pause before app launch

Turn on Pause before app launch to add a 10-second pause before a selected app or app category opens. The pause helps you reconsider whether you really need to use the app.

Privacy and security

App lock

Lock individual apps to keep them private. Locked apps require biometrics or your screen lock (PIN, pattern, or password) to open, and their widgets and notification content are hidden, even when someone has access to your unlocked phone.

Privacy display for secure app features (Ultra model only)

Privacy display can now turn on automatically for secure features, including Locked apps, Secret mode in Samsung Browser, private albums in Gallery, and locked notes in Samsung Notes. It also protects notifications panel and Recents previews from any app set to turn on Privacy display automatically.

Fingerprint and face recognition at the same time

Fingerprint and face recognition now work at the same time if you’ve registered both and the feature you’re using supports both verification types. You no longer need an extra tap to use face verification. Just look at the screen or touch the fingerprint sensor to verify your identity.

Redesigned biometric registration

Fingerprint and face registration screens have been redesigned with a cleaner, more refined look.

My Files

Improved document support

You can now open PPTX and DOCX files directly in My Files without installing Microsoft Office or other apps. Document Reader already supports PDF and TXT files.

Easier storage cleanup

When you manage storage in My Files, you now have the option to delete uncategorized and files that are in use in the Other category.

Samsung DeX

Optimized window maximizing

Maximizing a window now fills the entire screen, window controls are now integrated with the status bar at the top of the screen, and the apps background color is visible behind the taskbar at the bottom, providing a more immersive experience.

Auto split and more snap options

You can now snap windows to all four corners in addition to the top, bottom, left, and right. You can also arrange your running apps into 2, 3, or 4 split-screen windows at once.

Samsung Health

Enhanced sleep coaching

You can now start sleep coaching with just 3 days of data from the past two weeks. Check your overall sleep status and get personalized coaching tailored to your sleep patterns and goals.

Scan meals and log them instantly

Take a single photo of a meal before you eat it and get nutrition details, ingredients, and calorie estimates right away. No need to search for and enter every food you ate.

Mindful notes

Clear your mind and record your thoughts with free writing and guided prompts. Your notes sync seamlessly with Mood check-in to reveal your mood trends at a glance.

Track your medications worldwide

The Medications tracker is now available globally. You can enter your medications, set personalized reminders, and track your daily intake all in one place.

Reorder cards

You can now change the order of cards in the Activity, Sleep, Vitals, Mindfulness, and Nutrition tabs. Just drag and drop the cards you use the most to make them easier to find.

Accessibility

Intuitive floating accessibility shortcuts

Access your accessibility features from a floating button that’s always available, without the need to select additional options. Visual on and off indicators make it easy to see which features are available.

Improved hearing aid controls

Adjust your connected hearing aids’ volume from the notification panel. You can also choose which sounds from your phone reach your ears by opting out of notifications or ringtones and alarms.

Even more improvements

Search for Quick panel controls

When editing the Quick panel, you can search by app name or control name to find the controls you want quickly without scrolling through the full list.

Downloadable ringtones

Download past versions of Over the Horizon, Samsung’s signature sound, along with a curated selection of ringtones from past and present Samsung devices. Set any of them as your ringtone or use them for alarms.

Other changes

Audio brief and Moments no longer available

Audio brief and Moments will no longer be available in Now brief after you upgrade to One UI 9.5.

One UI 9.5 beta is available now for the Galaxy S26 series.

title: Best Buy brings back 4K Blu-ray discs with a slowly expanding collection
snippet: It’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game. more…
fullText:
It’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

As spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:

The Odyssey

Project Hail Mary

Interstellar

Saving Private Ryan

Obsession

Top Gun/Top Gun: Maverick two-pack

White Christmas

Speed Racer (2008)

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie

The Godfather

It’s a Wonderful Life

Supergirl (2026)

Masters of the Universe (2026)

Dr. Seuss’ How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000)

Technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023. 

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

title: Palmer Luckey doesn’t deny that he’s a prepper
snippet: The Anduril founder said Wednesday that Americans should always have three days of food, water, and medicine — just in case.
fullText:
Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst.

During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he said.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple, at Microsoft, at the NSA, and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has said that this is not the case, but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story.

“Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he said.  

Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.”

Luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.”

“What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked. 

Luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.”

However, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.”

“People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added.

It should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a new interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them.

title: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]
snippet: Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it? more…
fullText:
Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

Related: Samsung says Galaxy S26 vertical camera is a ‘core identity’ — it’s also a core problem

Finally, changes are incoming.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit. 

	

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

What do you think?

title: iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration
snippet: iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

iFixit tears Apple HomeView apart in more ways than one

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

	

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

title: YouTube Music removing Samples tab on Android & iOS
snippet: YouTube Music is simplifying its core navigation on Android and iOS by removing the Samples tab, though the vertical video format remains in the app. more…
fullText:
YouTube Music is simplifying its core navigation on Android and iOS by removing the Samples tab, though the vertical video format remains in the app.

The bottom bar is now just Home, Search, and Library for Premium subscribers. YouTube introduced the Samples feed in 2023 as a way to discover new songs via a Shorts-esque format. Tapping the tab opened a video player that cycled through the “latest release from an up-and-coming artist or a deep cut from a legacy artist” you might like.

While it’s no longer accessible from the navigation bar, Samples remains available on playlist, artist, and album pages in the top-right corner for a more focused experience.

This server-side change has been slowly rolling out in recent weeks, and we’re now seeing wider availability. For free users, “Upgrade” remains as a fourth tab. 

	

Meanwhile, YouTube Music has rolled out visual tweaks to buttons on the album and playlist pages. Play is now on the right, while download, add to library, and comments are grouped together at the left.

Looking ahead, YouTube announced in September that Ask Music will soon be accessible from the top-right corner. This Gemini spark icon is slowly rolling out to users.

title: Apple releases iOS 27.3 beta 2 for iPhone
snippet: Apple has released the second iOS 27.3 developer beta for iPhone. The upcoming software update includes the redesigned Health app, new Safari features, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the second iOS 27.3 developer beta for iPhone. The upcoming software update includes the redesigned Health app, new Safari features, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and more.

The second beta follows the first developer release on November 3 and first public beta on November 5.

One of the biggest changes introduced in iOS 27.3 so far is the redesigned Health app, which briefly appeared during iOS 27.2 testing before being removed ahead of release.

On supported iPhones, Health’s new Insights tab brings together trends from sleep, activity, and more. A new Longevity tab includes Health Age, which uses Apple Watch data to compare your health metrics with what’s typical for your age.

Other changes introduced in the first iOS 27.3 beta include:

Safari: Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode offer a new tab layout and a way to darken websites that don’t support Dark Mode.

Siri AI: New capabilities across Apple apps let you create and save Music playlists, schedule messages to send later, create Journal entries, and more.

iPhone Duo: Reachability shifts content horizontally toward either side of the display to make one-handed use easier.

StandBy: Updated clock faces bring more customization to other iPhones, including colors, complications, and multiple configurations.

Apple Fitness+: Gym Strength creates a four-week lifting plan based on your goals and available equipment.

Our full iOS 27.3 beta 1 roundup covers additional changes, including expanded Siri AI language support and Apple Music updates.

Developer beta testers can check for the update by opening Settings, choosing General, then Software Update. Select iOS 27 Developer Beta under Beta Updates.

Stay tuned as we update our devices and explore iOS 27.3 beta 2 for further changes. Find something new? Share your discoveries in the comments or email tips@9to5mac.com.

title: Google confirms huge list of new Home features, including three Nest Thermostat upgrades
snippet: Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the company is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade. more…
fullText:
Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the company is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to users.

The first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone. 

Google also says that Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers should see audio descriptions accompanying event descriptions from camera and doorbell events, including breaking glass or barking dogs. This adds more context to these already-useful alerts.

	

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and new keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six new countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

The first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat users in the US and Canada that shows “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Google explains:

Starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

A third update is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “New” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out new Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

title: Instagram launches dedicated ‘Direct’ messaging app that basically no one can use yet
snippet: Meta’s Instagram is launching a new “Direct” app that’s dedicated to direct messages, but it’s exceptionally limited at launch. more…
fullText:
Meta’s Instagram is launching a new “Direct” app that’s dedicated to direct messages, but it’s exceptionally limited at launch.

Available now on Android and iOS, “Direct” is a spinoff of Instagram’s direct messages. Instagram explains that the app is for “chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.” It uses the same framework as normal Instagram DMs, but is in its own app and has a few features not found in the Instagram app including:

Draw: Draw and sketch directly inside your chat threads.

Notes: Catch quick updates from friends right at the top of your inbox.

Stickers: Create custom stickers to express yourself and share with friends and family.

Voice Effects: Add fun audio effects like crowd laughter or underwater sounds to your replies.

Themes: Personalize your chat backgrounds with custom visual themes.

Meta says that “Direct” is available first in Türkiye and Thailand, and it doesn’t actually require an Instagram account. You can sign up with a phone number or email address, though this limits you to only being able to accept messages. Your contacts need to start the conversation with you, rather than allowing you to start conversations with others. Meta adds that “only your contacts and people you’re already connected to can start a chat with you or add you to a group on Direct,” and all users must be at least 13 years or older.

title: Ford Designed Its Fathom EV Battery Pack to Bend in a Crash, for Safety
snippet: Ford is designing the Fathom’s LFP battery to bend in a crash, not be shielded from one — and says the resulting EV will be safer and lighter for it.
fullText:
Ford’s new LFP battery pack isn’t a fragile electric car component that needs protection. During my visit this week to the automaker’s newly operational battery plant, engineers proudly showed me a video of the battery being crash-tested, the shell and the prismatic cells within bending violently under the force. My jaw practically hit the floor.

Conventional wisdom views an EV battery as a potentially explosive component that, if damaged, can cause catastrophic failure and hours-long fires that are difficult to extinguish. Years of lithium-ion batteries in phones, tablets and laptops taught us that and it’s largely held true for electric cars as well.

So the anxiety is well founded, even if, statistically, EVs are generally as safe as (if not safer than) internal combustion engine vehicles in crash testing and far less likely to catch fire.

			

More from CNET

‘The battery is not a jewel you must protect‘

Ford dropped that bombshell of a video on me at the end of my tour of its Blue Oval Battery Park outside Marshall, Michigan. However, I was barred from recording or photographing the footage.

The design team’s mantra was “don’t assume a cell must never deform.” For the upcoming Fathom and Ford’s Universal EV platform, or UEV, the pack is designed to carry up to 40% of side-impact forces and is treated as part of the vehicle’s crash structure. The company’s leadership and engineers are confident that the EV won’t catch fire or explode despite the bent cells.

Ford’s Fathom is yet to be revealed, but we’ve learned much about the electric truck ahead of its 2027 arrival.Ford

“Traditionally the battery is thought of as payload, a fragile jewel you must protect,” said Vladimir Bogachuk, chief engineer for advanced vehicle structure architecture at Ford. That approach, he said, means heavy bracing and protective structures around the pack. “The battery is not a jewel you must protect,” he said.

Bogachuk (along with every other Ford engineer and executive I spoke with that day) takes a less-is-more stance on the new EV platform. “The best part is no part,” he told me, “and if you have to have a part, it’s pretty much got to serve multiple functions.” And so the engineers set out to remove unnecessary armor and build a battery that serves double duty as an energy reservoir and crash structure.

Without that extra protection, the resulting EV can be lighter and more efficient, with improved driving dynamics. The UEV pack is deeply integrated into the vehicle’s structure: Its top lid is the cabin floor, and the seats bolt directly onto it. The bottom of the pack is the EV’s underbody. A service door beneath the Fathom’s rear seats will provide access to the charging and power electronics for service without the need to drop the pack.

The crash videos showed deformation that would scare me on an older EV, but when I stopped to think, it wasn’t much different from what I’ve seen in conventional car side-impact crash tests. Ford says an impact strong enough to deform the battery would also deform the chassis of a conventional vehicle or traditional EV, so the vehicle would likely be totaled anyway. More importantly, the engineers say the driver would be safe from thermal runaway and fire.

Cells and chemistry

When asked, Ford’s engineers said they don’t believe in a “right chemistry” for every electric vehicle. The UEV platform’s LFP — short for lithium iron phosphate — chemistry, prismatic cells and “jelly roll” construction were chosen for low manufacturing cost, resistance to temperature extremes, suitability for bidirectional energy use and the ability to deform while remaining inert under designed loads and forces.

Other automakers have floated solid-state batteries as a potential solution to battery safety and energy density, but the technology isn’t ready for use in production cars — at least not at the scale and price that Ford needs for the reasonably priced Fathom.

A pair of these so-called “jelly rolls” goes into each prismatic cell.Ford

Ford hasn’t stated the LFP pack’s energy capacity, the cell capacity or the number of cells the Fathom’s pack will comprise. Based on a cutaway displayed during my tour, I estimate 90 to 108 individual prismatic cells. The aluminum prismatic cans that enclose the cathode-anode “jelly roll” battery provide structural support and aid thermal dissipation throughout the larger pack.

Dedicated ‘abuse testing’ team

Wes Thibault, chief engineer for global energy storage systems, described the rigorous validation that the cells and packs underwent to reach the point where they can be trusted to bend like a taco. He told me that Ford has “a dedicated abuse-testing team” integrated with battery design and engineering at every level and stage of the manufacturing process, searching for edge cases and probing the limits of what the chemistry, the cells and full production-spec battery packs can take, from withstanding over 150,000 miles of simulated daily driving to remaining safe and inert in a crash. Along the way, CT scans of the cells offered an inside look at the jelly roll and how it was responding.

Ford’s testing covers structural integrity and load-bearing capability, heat soak from minus 40 to 60 degrees Celsius, IP67 water resistance and humidity cycling, and high-charge and high-discharge tests. For multiaxis vibration, the battery, seats and brackets are strapped to what I can describe only as a giant mechanical bull that shakes the hardware through roll, pitch, yaw and multiple harmonic frequencies. Ford can combine multiple factors in a single test, such as a high-humidity heat soak under vibration during high discharge.

Once the first batch of UEV vehicles are on the road, Ford says it’ll be able to capture real-world data from the fleet to further fine-tune its validation methods for future generations of EVs. 

Protect the passengers, not the battery

Given how well the first model year of Ford’s Mustang Mach-E‘s batteries have held up after six years and thousands of real-world miles, it’s clear the automaker knows a thing or two about building a reliable battery. 

The batteries in Ford’s Mach-E have proven surprisingly robust, but the automaker is asking much more from the UEV platform.Ford

That said, the UEV platform’s LFP chemistry and construction are very different from those of the earlier generation, and the automaker is asking much, much more of the pack than just holding and discharging energy. It’s asking the pack to actively protect the souls onboard in the event of a crash. Testing to failure early and learning from those mistakes quickly is something the engineers I spoke to seem to take very seriously.

This bold, out-of-the-box approach to how the automaker thinks about battery fragility — protecting the souls onboard rather than the “jewel” that is the battery from a potential crash at the end of the vehicle’s life — comes with the promise of more range and efficiency, less weight and more driving fun over the vehicle’s lifetime. 

I’m ready to believe. I want EV batteries to be safer and less scary. That promise depends heavily on whether the Fathom’s UEV battery pack is as safe as Ford says it is when it reaches driveways and dealerships in late 2027.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Ford. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Antuan Goodwin
						

						

							Senior Writer, Electrified Cars						
					

											

								

											Antuan has nearly 20 years of expertise and experience testing hundreds of cars, including electric, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and traditional combustion vehicles.

title: iPhone Duo now has twice as many optimized apps as it did 10 days ago
snippet: Apple marketing SVP Greg Joswiak said today that the number of iPhone Duo-ready apps on the App Store is twice what it was when Apple last reported the figure. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple marketing SVP Greg Joswiak said today that the number of iPhone Duo-ready apps on the App Store is twice what it was when Apple last reported the figure. Here are the details.

App Store crosses 200,000 iPhone Duo-optimized apps

While it was obvious that the number of iPhone Duo-ready apps would increase over time, their limited availability was a big part of the conversation around early reviews and online commentary in the first days after the device launched.

That said, it was clear even from the early reviews that app updates were picking up quickly, with some reviewers having to rewrite or re-record parts of their coverage as more apps gained support for the device.

Earlier this month, Apple put a number to that progress when it announced it had surpassed 100,000 optimized apps.

Now, just 10 days later, that number has doubled, according to Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak. In a post on X, he touted that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for iPhone Duo, adding that he is “excited by how quickly developers have embraced” the device.

Over 200,000 apps are now optimized for iPhone Duo! That number DOUBLED in just over a week.

I’m excited by how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and I can’t wait to see what they build next.

— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) November 16, 2026

Joswiak’s update came on the same day that Apple released iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, which addresses two other common complaints from early iPhone Duo reviews: the lack of Face ID, and the inability to automatically lock the device when closing it.

As 9to5Mac covered earlier today, the second developer beta of iOS 27.3 introduces a new unlock option that uses the outer display’s camera to recognize the user’s face, as well as a setting to automatically lock the device when folded shut.

The latter addresses a common complaint from users who found it strange that closing the phone didn’t automatically lock it, requiring them to press the side button instead.

For more details on these two features coming to the iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, follow this link.

title: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo
snippet: In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it. Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it. more…
fullText:
In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

Face unlock comes to iPhone Duo

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

In the Settings app, Apple says: 

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device. 

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Lock when closed

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

title: Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report
snippet: One Wall Street analyst got to the bottom of Nvidia's surprise announcement that it wouldn't be filing its formal quarterly results document, the 10-Q, for weeks.
fullText:
During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.

The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.

The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.

The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.

“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).

Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.

So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)

The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.

Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.

There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

title: Google Maps rolling out travel itineraries & list search for Ask Maps
snippet: Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other new capabilities for Ask Maps. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the holiday season, Google Maps is launching a handy travel itineraries feature alongside a slew of other new capabilities for Ask Maps.

Ask Maps can now build travel itineraries that feature numbered map pins for each stop. It supports everything from shopping excursions to multi-day road trips with several stops. When used for the latter, Google Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with tips and the numbered pins that aid visualization. Plans can be shared with others and exported to Google Docs on desktop. 

Once on the trip, Ask Maps will show directions and real-time details, including live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and “even what the vibe is at your next stop.” You can conversationally have Google add more stops to the itinerary.

Meanwhile, Ask Maps can now tap into your saved lists to find bookmarked places and take action. This lets you ask: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” 

	

Before you start directions, you’ll see familiar “Know Before You Go” tips that surface information about your route, like parking locations, car charging options, weather, potential delays, and tolls.

New agentic capabilities let Ask Maps find online beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, as well as call local businesses on your behalf. For example, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me” returns a list of open slots.

Finally, Ask Maps is expanding to 30 more countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK.

These updates are rolling out starting today on Google Maps for Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and list search are available in all 200+ Ask Maps countries. Know Before You Go in directions and appointment booking are coming first to the US.

title: You can now set up Gemini’s Google Wallet integration for ‘personal finance insights’
snippet: As we spotted in September, the Gemini app is adding Google Wallet integration in the US that makes possible “responses informed by your spending habits.” more…
fullText:
As we spotted in September, the Gemini app is adding Google Wallet integration in the US that makes possible “responses informed by your spending habits.”

In the Gemini app, @Google Wallet allows you to: 

Visualize spending: Questions like “can we review my spending from last quarter so I can save $1,000 over the next three months?” enable Gemini to generate dynamic charts tracking cash flow, asset allocation, and budgets directly in your chat.

Find forgotten subscriptions: If you ask “what subscriptions am I still paying for, and did any of them go up in price this year?” Gemini finds recurring charges across your linked accounts and flags price increases.

Budget for the holidays: When you ask “how much did I spend on gifts and travel last year? Use that to help me set a holiday budget for this year,” Gemini will look at your transactions from the last year and suggest a budget tailored to you.

The interactive visualizations (seen above) are quite cool. This integration leverages third-party service Plaid to “securely link your financial accounts from your credit cards and banks” to Google Wallet.

On the privacy front, this integration is read-only, with Gemini not able to “move, manage, or invest your money.”

	

You decide if and when you want to opt in to this experience, and you can turn the connection on or off at any time. Learn more here.

Once enabled, @Google Wallet is available in the Gemini app on Android, iOS, and web for US users. To get started, go to Customize > Connectors or gemini.google.com/customize/connectors.

Google bills this as an expansion of Personal Intelligence, which already taps into Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube to customize responses. The company today also highlighted the launch of Memory Summary from earlier this week.

fullText:

Here’s what to expect from iPhone 20 Pro and iPhone Duo 2, per latest leaks

Rumors for next year’s flagship new iPhone models are ramping up. Earlier today, we got a release timing update on iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 and learned that Apple may have multiple iPhone 20 Pro designs in testing.

Now more details have arrived via Weibo leakers Digital Chat Station and Fixed Focus Digital, who focus on the highly-anticipated new iPhone Pro models and also the iPhone Duo 2.

Apple used titanium for the iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, then abandoned it with the 17 Pro and 18 Pro. Titanium is used on the iPhone Air though. With next year’s 20th anniversary Pro models taking design cues from the Air, it sounds like titanium could return.

	

Leaker Digital Chat Station, in a reply to this post about iPhone Duo 2, adds that the 20 Pro series will be larger in size and have a bezel-free, quad-curved display.

Regarding the Duo 2, he says it will have the same 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer display as the first model. The side button with integrated Touch ID remains unchanged as well.

On the possibility of Face ID being added, he says it’s “questionable.” He suggests internal components might require too many changes, but doesn’t offer inside information.

title: Oppo may finally be fixing broken 3rd-party launchers with ColorOS 17
snippet: Most Chinese-brand Android phones don’t like it when you use a 3rd-party launcher, but the ColorOS 17 update may be changing that. more…
fullText:
Most Chinese-brand Android phones don’t like it when you use a 3rd-party launcher, but the ColorOS 17 update may be changing that.

If I hop on a phone from Oppo, Vivo, Honor, or most other Chinese brands and try to use a 3rd-party launcher, I’m definitely not going to like how the phone operates. Often, there’s a weird delay when navigating back home or opening the Overview multitasking screen. Sometimes, Overview doesn’t work at all, essentially forcing you back to the default launcher that shipped with the phone.

But one Reddit user says Oppo is doing things differently in the ColorOS 17 update. According to their experience, the delay and other issues with 3rd-party launchers are completely solved. OnePlus’s OxygenOS doesn’t have the same issues, so it’s good to see that OnePlus users who are still set to receive ColorOS 17 in the near future won’t feel like their phones are losing a valuable feature.

Chinese Android brands like Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Realme, and several others often outshine Western brands in many ways, but they’ve always had one annoying weakness: software. Whether it’s the number of updates a phone receives, overall quality, or another specific issue, Chinese brands often build very different visions of Android than Google, Samsung, Motorola, or Nothing.
