title: Google Home speakers get a major Gemini upgrade ‘soon,’ but only for paid subscribers
snippet: Google has confirmed that a big update is in store for the Gemini experience on Google Home speakers, but it’ll only be available to paid subscribers. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a big update is in store for the Gemini experience on Google Home speakers, but it’ll only be available to paid subscribers.

Alongside the huge list of new updates Google detailed yesterday, the company also announced that a “faster and more natural” version of Gemini Live is coming to speakers and smart displays “soon.”

Google explains this is from Gemini Live moving to the “latest speech-to-speech architecture” and brings “significantly faster response times.” Gemini Live isn’t the default experience when you start a “Hey Google” command, rather hiding behind a “let’s chat” or other similar command to start a session. 

Initially, Live sessions were purely for brainstorming or longer conversations and lacking support for commands and other functions mid-session, but Google now says that this upgrade will add support for actions such as smart home controls, setting timers, and more without leaving a Live session. That’s a big deal.

	

Google explains:

Coming soon – A faster and more natural Gemini Live experience: Available with a Google Home Premium subscription, Gemini Live is being upgraded to our latest speech-to-speech architecture for significantly faster response times and a smoother experience. Just say, “Hey Google, let’s chat” to brainstorm dinner ideas or plan a trip out loud, interrupt naturally to change topics, and perform actions mid-conversation—such as, setting a timer, adding a reminder,or controlling a smart home device—without stepping out of the chat³.

The “catch” is that you’ll still need a subscription to use this. Gemini Live has always required a subscription on Google Home speakers and smart displays, with the functionality looped into Google Home Premium plans which start at $10/month (or bundled into Google One AI Pro). That’s the same subscription that gives you Nest storage.

title: Did Christopher Nolan Just Bring 4K Blu-Ray Discs Back to Stores?
snippet: The Odyssey hit the shelves of Best Buy, just in time for the holidays.
fullText:
Physical media lovers, take note: Best Buy has begun selling 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray discs in-store and online. If you’ve been paying attention, you’ll know how big a pivot this is for the electronics retailer. Back in 2023, the company announced it would cease all sales of DVDs and Blu-rays entirely.

Now, thanks to Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster phenom and Oscar frontrunner The Odyssey, which is the first-ever movie to be filmed entirely on IMAX cameras, the company is once again stocking its shelves with Blu-rays. Right now, you’ll find only copies of the Greek epic in store (with a small selection of other titles available for purchase directly through the retailer’s online store), and that makes sense considering how popular it was in theaters and how awesome it will look on big TVs at home.

Matt Damon stars as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s three-hour epic, The Odyssey.Universal Pictures

But this move also raises the question: Will other 4K and standard Blu-rays be coming to Best Buy stores in the near future?

			

More from CNET

A Best Buy spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

When the retailer first announced it would be ditching DVD and Blu-ray sales, it cited the decades-long decline in physical media sales — which fell from its peak revenue benchmark of $16 billion in 2005 to less than $1 billion in 2024 — and planned to populate the store space with other tech-based products.

The Odyssey, the nearly 3-hour-long big-screen adaptation of Homer’s epic poem, follows King Odysseus (played by Matt Damon) as he leads his soldiers on a 10-year journey home after the Trojan War. It features a stacked slate of acting talent from Anne Hathaway and Tom Holland to Zendaya, Jon Bernthal and Charlize Theron, and earned $1.8 billion at the global box office.

Those details, along with the timing of the coming holiday shopping season, have apparently inspired Best Buy to change course. 

It should be noted that physical media still has value for many people. In an era when movies and TV shows (purchased or otherwise) are suddenly pulled from streamers, the allure of owning titles on DVD and Blu-ray endures. Not to mention, 4K Blu-rays offer better picture quality than their compressed, streaming versions.

fullText:
Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Halide 3.4 adds a bigger viewfinder and fill flash for iPhone Duo

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

title: Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps
snippet: Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

Microsoft sets June 30 shutdown date for To Do on Mac and iPhone

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House
snippet: A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state. All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest … more…
fullText:
A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest … 

	

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected. 

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

title: How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator
snippet: macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another. If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround. more…
fullText:
macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain

sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

Not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. Terminal command + reboot removed.

title: Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects
snippet: Following a preview at Google I/O, Google is rolling out 66 new regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean. more…
fullText:
Following a preview at Google I/O, Google is rolling out 66 new regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean.

For users in the UK, the update brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences. The lineup includes Geordie, Scouse, Brummie, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish, Modern RP, and Multicultural London English (MLE).

This might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents, in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live. We have not yet been able to test to confirm this has been resolved with the update. As someone with a regional English accent, this extra representation with Gemini voices is quite welcome.

According to Google, these voices are tuned for natural pronunciation, pitch, and everyday local rhythm rather than exaggerated stereotypes. Because the focus is on cadence over slang, Gemini will sound like a local without filling its text responses with forced street slang. Once selected, your chosen voice carries across the entire app, applying to both Gemini Live conversations and standard text-to-speech playback when tapping the “Listen” icon on chat responses.

	

You can preview and select the new options today by tapping the three-dot menu inside Gemini Live, or by heading into the Gemini app settings and selecting “Gemini’s voice.” It’s worth noting that the voices aren’t explicitly labeled by city or region in the app menu, and Gemini isn’t programmed to self-identify which accent it is using if you ask it directly.

Instead, Google notes that locally rooted prompts about food, culture, or sport, such as asking for the best pub in Sheffield for a Sunday roast – my suggestion is not a pub; it’s Turnip & Thyme on Eccleshall Road, FWIW. Or another suggestion from big G is where to find proper ingredients for a traditional Scouse stew; the company says these will naturally bring out the warmth and rhythm of the new dialects.

I’d suggest trying to ask where to get the best pattie and chips in Hull or where to get the best pint in Leeds (it’s Whitelocks).

fullText:
Stevie Bonifield

ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.

Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.

snippet: First appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do. more…
fullText:
First appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do.

Rolling out now via what appears to be a server-side update (tied to Google Play Services), Google Pixel phones are adding a “Family” section to the Settings menu. The feature is appearing for us on a Pixel 11 Pro XL running the October 2026 update (not Android 17 QPR2), while a Pixel 10 Pro has also just surfaced the new UI.

This new section, which Google has previously referred to as “Family Hub,” gives users a quick place to see their family members and settings in one central location. It shows a list of your family members – child accounts and anyone attached to your Google One family plan – with controls over Google One storage, Google Play Family Library, shared payment methods, and “Family events” in Google Calendar.

You can also see the live location of any family members you are sharing your location with or start sharing your location with another family member. You can also easily remove or add members to your family plan via this new menu. Each family member gets their own page where you can see benefits shared, location, and also if they are a “parent” in the family – with “remove” and “transfer” options available.

	

	

While this won’t be helpful for all users, it’s certainly full of useful shortcuts and tools for those at the center of a family plan and looking to share benefits with their household. 

As far as we can tell, this is widely rolled out to Pixel owners at this point. As mentioned, we’re seeing it across multiple devices, and 9to5Google readers mentioned they’re also seeing it live even prior to installing the latest system update. The folks at Droid-Life also mention now seeing it on their Pixels.

title: Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027
snippet: Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience. more…
fullText:
Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables. 

Referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments. 

Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store. 

At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing new apps or updating your store listing.”

	
	

By August 2027, new and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”

Tier 2: Adaptive optimized — Evaluates responsive multi-pane layouts, avoiding stretched UI elements, as well as basic support for external keyboard, mouse, trackpad, and stylus input across foldables, tablets, and other large screen devices.

Tier 1: Adaptive differentiated — Evaluates tabletop and book postures, camera continuity, interactive picture-in-picture, and multi-instance support for media, video, reading, and multitasking apps.

Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”

On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

Tier 3: Ready: The baseline required for seamless play on foldables and tablets. Games render full screen in their supported orientation(s) with unobstructed HUD safe areas, cleanly letterbox or pillarbox in-engine when rotated to an unsupported orientation, and preserve state and touch alignment across folding, unfolding, rotation, and multi- window resizing.

Tier 2: Optimized: Builds on Tier 3 to deliver an elevated experience across foldables and tablets, featuring high-resolution graphics and proportional HUD scaling, styled visual framing when letterboxing, smooth frame pacing, and full playability with external controllers, keyboards, and mice.

Tier 1: Differentiated : Defines flagship showcase experiences tailored to each form factor. On foldables, Tier 1 focuses on sustained high-frame-rate performance (60 FPS, and 120 FPS on supported displays), thermal and battery stability across extended unfolded sessions, efficient modern graphics rendering, and dynamic resolution scaling between inner and cover screens.

title: iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a convenient new setting, here’s how to use it
snippet: iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

iOS 27 adds new slider in Control Center to fine-tune your AirPods Adaptive Audio

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). 

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options. 

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

title: MagSafe Monday: MOFT’s Trackable Field Wallet holds eight cards, cash, and supports Find My
snippet: The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app. more…
fullText:
The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

The wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

MOFT Trackable Field Wallet capacity and stand

The wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

The stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

Two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

Wrap up on MOFT Trackable Field Wallet

I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is the other end of that accessory spectrum: more cards, a stand, and Find My built in. If Find My is the reason you’ve stuck with Apple’s wallet, this is a really nice option that holds a bunch and is trackable.

The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from MOFT.

title: YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now
snippet: Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count. more…
fullText:
Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change. 

	

YouTube says it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”

How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”

YouTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

This change is rolling out now.

title: Samsung Galaxy’s next major update keeps leaking – here’s what to expect in One UI 9.5
snippet: Samsung is preparing its next major update for Galaxy phones, One UI 9.5, and new details have been coming to light. Here’s an overview of a lot of One UI 9.5 updates that have leaked so far. more…
fullText:
Samsung is preparing its next major update for Galaxy phones, One UI 9.5, and new details have been coming to light. Here’s an overview of a lot of One UI 9.5 updates that have leaked so far.

One UI 9.5 will still be based on Android 17, but it’s set to be packed with various changes based on recent leaks. In particular, it seems like Samsung has a ton of new AI features in store.

“Galaxy Claw” is supposedly Samsung’s new “personal agent,” able to leverage apps on your device including your notifications, Contacts, Gmail, Messages, and more. Specifically, Android Authority reports it will be able to use Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone, and Voice Recorder, with the agent able to set up scheduled tasks. It does sound like this will be a paid feature, though, with Samsung’s new $4.99/month AI Premium plan. There would also be a new dashboard for showing AI usage.

There’s also a new Memory feature in Bixby that would let the assistant reference past details from conversations or commands. 

	

Daily Brief, sharing its name with Google’s canceled Pixel feature, would be able to summarize notifications from various apps, grouping cards into “Finance and payments,” “Bookings and appointments,” and “Work email,” though that list seems incomplete. 

It’s not all about AI. It also looks like Samsung’s Expert RAW camera experience is being improved with better labels, customizable buttons, a screen lock option, burst mode support, and more. It even seems like there’s video support coming.

Other new features that have leaked include:

Custom greetings in Call Screening

“Meal Scan” for calorie counts/macros based on photos

Contact widgets with AI-powered call summaries, replies, etc

Tap to Share (already available on Pixel)

Search button in the Phone app

Birthday section in Samsung’s Contacts app

Rambler-like voice-to-text in Samsung Keyboard

“Play-on” integrates notifications and messages from games into Now Brief, more

One UI 9.5 will almost certainly be launching on next year’s Galaxy S27 series before expanding to more devices later on, as has been the case for the past several updates. A beta program will likely be available on Galaxy S26 series soon – the One UI 8.5 beta program opened up in early December 2025.

title: Samsung’s ‘Galaxy Studio’ headphones leak with touch controls, two colors
snippet: We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some new leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the company’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising. more…
fullText:
We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some new leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the company’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising.

Samsung hasn’t produced over-ear headphones in about a decade — under its own name, at least — but it looks like that’s about to change. We hadn’t heard much in the way of details on the company’s next audio release, rumored to be named ‘Galaxy Studio,’ but a fresh leak courtesy of SamMobile is finally changing that. We’ll have to keep waiting for full renders, but these leaked graphics are giving us a general idea of what they might look like, plus a couple of key features.

Unsurprisingly, Galaxy Studio will include ANC, complete with a dedicated button to toggle the setting between its usual modes. Volume controls also could come in the shape of physical buttons, but playback controls appear to be relegated to a touch-sensitive area on its earpads, something that’s become relatively standard among the flagship headphone competition. SamMobile also reports it’ll come in “at least” black and red colorways, while a leak from earlier this month suggested rotational earcups.

Okay, is it me or is the random goatee in this graphic crazy?

Again, I don’t want to read too much into these leaked graphics, as it’s always possible the final release has a handful of changes. Based on these images, though, I’m pleasantly surprised to see Samsung avoiding an attempt at copying Apple’s AirPods Max design. The larger cups, combined with their ability to twist and turn for easy storage, sounds much closer to most (but not all) of Sony’s over-ear efforts across the last decade or so, and when it comes to headphones, there are much, much worse choices you could look to for inspiration. If Samsung can hit the right price on these — or bundle them with one of their ever-more-expensive smartphones — they could be a real winner.

title: AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

GymKit can sync AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate data

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

Siri AI

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

World Knowledge: “Ask about virtually any topic that’s on your mind, from important facts to recipes and restaurant recommendations. Siri AI can reference information online to give you detailed, up-to-date insights.”

Conversational: “Siri AI is your conversational AI assistant with entirely new capabilities…Ask open-ended questions, brainstorm ideas for work or creative projects on the go, and engage in natural, back-and-forth conversations.”

Personal Context: “Siri AI can find relevant answers to what you’re looking for just by asking. Search for a photo from years ago, easily locate an email buried in your inbox, or pull up a note you saved on your iPhone.”

Precision Finding via Apple Watch

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

title: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free
snippet: Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free. more…
fullText:
Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch. 

	

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

title: Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock
snippet: Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

Arthur Levinson’s stock sales are not unusual

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

snippet: Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale. Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … more…
fullText:
Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … 

	

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

They heard the feedback: Apple is testing the return of iOS 26’s softer scroll-edge effect in navigation bars when glass tint is set to 25% or lower.

Currently disabled behind UIKit/clear_glass_soft_pocket. Applies to the default/auto style. pic.twitter.com/D2NvKfESYa

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 16, 2026

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

title: How Silicon Valley lost the public, with Crooked Media’s Jon Favreau
snippet: Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country. Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem. That’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public? Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio. But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members. So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view. Of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the issue. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks for having me, Nilay. I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation. I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator company in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks. What do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans said, “No, we still see through it.” I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?” And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.” You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics. Is it just that simple? I hate that it’s that simple. It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?” We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it. It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House. The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good. We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work. So they said, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics. Is there some reason the incumbent party does not realize that saying something that sounds like “the fundamentals of the economy are strong” kills you? Because you’re describing a pattern that repeats and it’s that phrase almost exactly. Yes. That’s why we understood it once 2012 rolled around because people were still not satisfied with the economy when Obama was running for reelection and we did everything we could to make that election a choice. We acknowledged that people were still struggling and people were still in pain. We totally avoided the long list of statistics about how wonderful the economy was getting and how everyone had recovered and all that kind of stuff. We just said, “Look, things are still rough out there, but it’s a choice. This is the kind of vision Mitt Romney has for the economy and this is the vision we have for the economy. You get to pick one.” There’s a way, if you are the incumbent party in power, to still keep people on your side, but you’ve got to at least acknowledge and be honest about how people are feeling. You can’t tell people to feel a way that they aren’t feeling. You can’t tell people that a whole bunch of issues are important that aren’t the issues that matter most to them in their lives or at least to most people, which is, “Do I feel economically secure and do I actually feel safe?” That’s why people care about crime and they care about safety in their communities and then they also care about whether they can afford gas and groceries. The one issue that really struck me in that framework is surveillance. We’ve done a number of episodes about Flock cameras and AI-enabled surveillance and the idea that you can just link all the databases together and Palantir can send a drone to your house to murder you. That connects directly to safety. The CEO of Ring has been on the show and his argument is, “If I put up enough Ring cameras, I will zero out crime in certain neighborhoods.” I’ve asked him about the mechanism of how that will exactly work and the answer is that the thieves will be deterred by surveillance. It’s the same for the CEO of Flock. It’s the same argument everywhere. “If we just watch you enough, we’ll stop crime.” The American public hates this idea. There’s some limit to how much crime-stopping you want compared to how much surveillance must occur. I watched the CEO of Flock in particular try to go hard MAGA in this election cycle and use the phrase, “The radical leftists want a crime world,” or whatever it is he was saying, and it just didn’t work. That to me felt like a glimmer of a realignment where the libertarians in America were saying, “No, we still don’t want a state with this level of power,” and your classic ACLU Democrats were saying, “Yep, that’s pretty bad,” and then throw all the bumps out, like, “Just get out of here and we’ll start over.” What do you make of that? Because there are other glimmers of realignment, but that is the one that really stuck out to me. It’s interesting. I do think privacy is the other issue that affects people personally, that they can feel. You go through your life and if you lose your privacy, then there’s public shaming and embarrassment — there’s a violation there. So at least in people’s minds, they still do balance safety and security with privacy concerns. We have that in so many aspects of life. Their social media presence was mostly TikTok, mostly Instagram, and it was just James Talarico telling stories really. It was giving speeches, but it was some of the oldest stories in human history, like David and Goliath. But I do think that [concerning] the whole “politicians as content creators” thing, there’s a way to do it where you are participating in the circus and then there’s a way to do it that is true to yourself and your values and the story you want to tell about where the country is and where you want to take it. If that story is compelling, then it will travel and break through even in this crowded media environment. The rise of vertical video allows for that kind of storytelling in a way that we haven’t seen in a while. After Barack Obama won the Iowa caucuses, we knew that every primary night he would get primetime coverage when he won and would be able to deliver a message to the whole country because everyone would be watching because it was primary night. We really focused on those speeches. For Talarico’s campaign, and for a lot of these other Democrats now, they have a million of those moments every day, but they still have to do the storytelling in order for it to break through. The most successful candidates figured out how to do that storytelling in a really compelling way that wasn’t just “I’m going to tell a joke on Twitter” or “I’m going to do the hype reel” if I’m the House Oversight Committee. That is an effective way of getting people’s attention, but not necessarily holding their attention. If you are a politician today, you’ve got to figure out a way to get people’s attention, but then to hold it. And to hold it, you have to have a compelling story to tell. My favorite piece of election day media was Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa doing the Fleetwood Mac video where he drank the cranberry juice and longboard. I thought, this is great. I don’t know what the purpose of this video is, but I’m having a good time. And maybe that’s all you needed on this day was to just channel some vibes. Then you got to actually go make some policy proposals. You have to fill potholes in New York City and then sit there and make videos about the filled potholes, which the Mamdani administration is particularly good at doing. Do you think this class of Democrats has that ability, even though they have a president who’s threatening to veto everything that they’re going to do? I do think they have the ability. They’re going to be able to communicate. They’re going to be able to have hearings when they’re holding big tech CEOs and administration officials accountable. Those will be moments. They’re going to also have moments where they get to exert power over the government funding process. I personally think we’ll be headed towards several shutdowns because that’s going to be the main mechanism for Democrats to get their way. But also for the next two years, Donald Trump and the Congress are just not going to be the main focus. The main storyline of the next two years is going to be the presidential primaries. I remember Democrats had a huge win in 2006, and then people can barely remember until the financial crisis what George Bush and the Democratic Congress were up to between 2006 and 2008, because everyone was focused on the Republican primary for president and the Democratic primary for president, because they were two wide open primaries. Once we get into 2027, you’re going to have a million primary debates on both sides. Donald Trump’s obviously going to try to insert himself into the debate by trying to play kingmaker on the Republican side so that he can continue to get attention. And God forbid there are external events and crises that we have to deal with, then everyone’s going to be paying attention to Trump and the Congress. But the machinations of what’s happening inside the Congress I think will be the secondary story of the next two years. You mentioned tech regulation. Actually, that’s where I want to end. I’ve often described hearings in Congress with tech CEOs as content capture sessions. That’s what we’re doing. Instead of Apple having the new iPhone and all the creators rushing in to take photos of it, here’s Mark Zuckerberg and all the senators are going to rush to yell at him and we all make our videos and that’s the end of that. Nothing ever seems to happen. Our audience is particularly nihilistic about it. You can yell at these CEOs all you want, but they just get their own way. There’s a lot of opportunity for oversight, particularly around AI, particularly Jensen Huang, the opportunity to do oversight over Nvidia and the Commerce Department and the FBI, whatever is happening. Boy, is there a lot of opportunity to oversight there. How do you think that looks? We cover this often from a technology lens on the show. You cover it from a political lens on Offline. What do you think this looks like? I know what I want it to look like. Because of where we are with AI development, I am more interested in oversight that actually changes the situation, that finally puts some guardrails or restrictions on the development of super intelligence, AGI, recursive self-improvement, whatever you want to call it, than just show trials where we all get to dunk on Mark Zuckerberg. My biggest concern is we don’t have time to wait for a Democratic president or even a Republican president who’s actually going to do something to regulate the development of AI because by the time we get to 2028, it feels like the horse will have well left the barn. It’s already left the barn. I’m curious, over the next two years, can Democrats and Republicans in Congress actually force some kind of regulation or at least coordination among the AI giants to stop us from going off the cliff here? If I had to point to a realignment, it’s what I mentioned at the top. Surveillance feels like a glimmer of a realignment, and then data centers and AI feel like the glimmers of a realignment. You shouldn’t just take the economy away from people. Regardless of partisan lean, I think for most people, to your point about agency, feel you can’t just do that. You have to show up and make the case. That is enough for a wholesale realignment. Those two issues are enough for these parties to totally scramble. And you’re going to get pro-business Democrats saying, “We’re going to have to do something to work with these guys.” You’re already seeing it. There’s James Talarico saying, “I wish Elon would just stay in his lane and stay out of politics, but we need him as a great businessman.” You’re seeing it on the Republican side: “We got this wrong. We need to regulate the Big Tech companies. I’m anti-data center too.” In this environment where they basically have a little less than a year to make headway before the primary cycles begin, what do you think the steps are? I worry that when I listen to a lot of these Democratic politicians and Republican politicians, all of them, there’s only a handful that seem to really understand the technology. You talk about regulation with people and they say, “Yeah, we need safeguards.” Safeguards could be anything from its effect on children and chatbots to making sure that we don’t lose human control of artificial intelligence. I feel like the cybersecurity stuff and the bio stuff — and then where recursive self-improvement goes — are the big areas where I would want to see Democrats and Republicans get together. Even if they can’t pass laws because Trump doesn’t want to do anything to hurt the AI companies because he looks at it and says, “The stock market’s tied to this, the economy’s tied to this, and I don’t want to do anything to hurt the economy and got to beat China and all that bullshit” — which is not bullshit — but you can’t answer every single concern about runaway artificial intelligence and losing control with the word “China.” Trump seems to be doing that and some other politicians as well. But he can’t anymore because there are Chinese spies. [Laughs] Right. He’ll try. He’s going to try. This is going to change the terms of this debate. An empowered set of China hawks are saying, “Look at the spies.” But even if there were no spies, they also lifted the export controls before to send the chips to China. Because of the sexy spies. It’s right there. But it was also probably in their financial interest, even if there were no sexy spies. I do think that even if you can’t get regulations passed, there needs to be even the convening power of the federal government with these companies to sit them all in a room and say, “We have to work on this together.” And international diplomacy with the Chinese. We’re not going to get out of this in one piece by Trump and Xi meeting and saying, “Yeah, it was a great meeting and we both think AI is important and we’re going to keep talking about it.” You have to actually get down into the details and the weeds here over the next two years or else I think things could get really bad really fast. I can hear our audience screaming in their cars. I can predict their YouTube comments. The YouTube AI should just start doing predicted comments. No, I’m worried it’s not going to happen. I’m with it. They’re screaming nihilism at you. They’re saying, “None of this will happen.” I worry about the same thing. I think public pressure around this is the only avenue here right now, as long as Trump’s in power. People inside the companies, people outside the companies continue to talk about this to raise the alarm, to sound the alarm on this and to tell people about the dangers. I don’t think that’s necessarily going to get us to the best place, but it’s the best chance that we have right now. My hottest election take has been that this election proved that X is irrelevant, that Elon Musk’s purchase of X is now a failure on every dimension. It’s shrunken users. He’s definitely not making as much money as even failed Jack Dorsey Twitter used to make. Again, criticism of Elon’s X is in no way praise of the Jack Dorsey Twitter. That was a poorly run company that allowed this outcome to happen, but it’s not making more money. It doesn’t have more users. And now we can see the absolute limit of its political influence. Yeah. It has outsized influence on the political debate because of all of the journalists and politicians who are on it. What we saw in the last cycle is the limits of the political debate to influence the decision of the electorate. I would connect that to the people at these companies needing to keep raising the alarm because the place where they keep raising the alarm is on X and they’re not great communicators when it comes to the public. They can’t make the case for data centers. In fact, mostly what the public hears is, “We might kill all of you.” Another anonymous researcher has surfaced to say that they’re quitting their job instead of killing you all. Now what? Do you think that there’s a better way to make that jump to make that case? Yes, because every time I see one of these posts — I just saw someone who said, “I just came from San Francisco and I’m so scared. This is crazy,” and I said, “All right” — but then there’s never a good explanation for most people as to why. What is the scary part? San Francisco is just Milwaukee with rich people. I need to make this as clear as I can. It is not as scary as people want it to be. But I do think that there is — speaking of storytelling — a storytelling function missing here where it’s great that people are speaking out and saying this is dangerous, but then you want to say, “Okay, how is it dangerous? Give us the steps from recursive self-improvement to the robots killing us all, or robots don’t have to kill us all, but [they can create] a horrible cyber attack or biological weapons.” I do think painting the picture of actually how this could affect people and continuing to sound the alarm on that and then saying, “If we did these things, we might be able to slow this down or stop it” is important too. Because if you’re just going to scare people without providing a path to how to fix the problem or how to rein it in, then eventually, it’s just going to be noise. “Oh, another person’s screaming about how we’re all going to die. What am I going to do about that?” There’s some very basic political science in here. Why we have a government is to counterbalance industry. Again, are we telling stories on social media? Abdul El-Sayed is doing political science 101 — “I’m a capitalist.” Adam Smith is like “monopoly is a danger to capitalism,” and this is eighth grade. He’s just doing eighth grade at people all the time to explain that the role of government is to constrain industry in some way or provide some sort of framework for industry to make lives better for people instead of just collecting profits. That is the role of government. AI is the ultimate collective action problem or prisoner’s dilemma, whatever you want to call it. It is why we have governments, not just a government in our country, but why we have the United Nations and an international order of countries that even if they don’t agree, even if they are adversaries, can sit down and figure things out together because there are just some problems that none of us can solve on our own. There are some set of Republicans who say, “We should go back to being free markets. We should go back to this thing.” Do you think that they are going to have any influence in this next turn? No. Fair enough. They might have influence. A lot of them have finally realized that they have lost the public on this. I was interested to hear the All In pod after the election, and Chamath Palihapitiya especially, talking about, “We thought that maybe everyone would trust that if the asset managers and the rich people did well, they would ultimately do well. That’s clearly not the case.” It’s like, “Yeah, obviously.” But I think a lot of them just didn’t realize that. That was the longest winded, most VC coded version of the voodoo economic speech I ever heard. It was. It is wild. I’m like, “You’re just getting that now? Oh, cool. Great.” “We’re just saying trickle down didn’t work again, but in this way.” Okay, that’s fine. That ecosystem is closed. It is. I’m thinking of Andrew Sullivan warning the Republican Party of epistemic closure in 2000 on his blog on The Atlantic. And now we’ve landed at a closed podcast ecosystem where I’m pretty confident everyone’s buying views for each other, just to be clear, to make it look bigger and more influential than it is. But the fever has to break there too. The CEOs can’t all just be creators. They have to run their companies and make their shareholders money and operate in a new political environment. How does that fever break? Silicon Valley has always been incredibly insular like this. Even back in the social media age, even when we dealt with them in government. I got to know some of these folks afterwards when I moved out here. They view everyone who works in government as, “Politics is just an engineering problem to solve. The fact that it’s this messy means you must be a bunch of dummies running the place.” This is the theory behind DOGE. “If we can just go in there and bring our technology and bring our brilliance, we should solve all these political problems.” But political problems are problems of the human condition. It’s people trying to figure out how to live together and divvy up scarce resources and figure out how to govern themselves. That’s really messy and you actually need some social and political expertise to do that. You can’t just be a genius coder or a capitalist and feel like this is going to solve everything. But I think for a long, long time in Silicon Valley, they’ve seen the government as just another problem to be solved by engineering or capital allocation. And it’s just not. It’s never going to be that. Politics is going to be much messier. I think it’s all of that. And then one I would add to it is they also see it as a rich source of revenue, which is why you have seen so many of them move into being defense contractors. It’s an inarguable way to get a bunch of money from the government, to say, “We will build you weapons and AI systems for blah, blah, blah.” All of them have done it regardless of their professed values. The idea that YouTube is run by a defense contractor is mind-blowing to me. I know. But it is just straightforwardly true, right? Yeah. You can see the idea that SpaceX is a defense contractor and we might turn down Starlink in Ukraine and Trump has to go on television and be like, “I have no idea what happened.” Right, and Elon’s just sitting there saying, “I can flip a switch whenever I want.” Yeah, there’s something there. Again, to come back to collective action problems and the role of government to actually control these companies and control the industry. It seems like it’s up for grabs in a way that suggests you and I should probably talk again very soon. It feels like in these next two years, that realignment, the glimmers of it that I see are either going to come true or not. I’ve been wrong before, but something about the relationship between government and the tech industry is bound to change. I agree. Jon, this has been great. What’s next for Crooked? Tell people what to look out for. We just finished Crooked Con, which was wildly successful. We had over 3,000 people to talk about the results of the election, and now we’re just trying to figure out how to cover this primary. You’re already in primary coverage? The primary has begun. Even though people have not announced their candidacies yet, by the time we get to winter, it’s going to be in full swing. So DeSantis, Rubio and JD. Ted Cruz. Oh, God. I know, and then a million people on the Democratic side. You’re already covering it. All right. I was hopeful that we would get some sincere legislative action, but we’re doing primaries. We’ll do both. It’s going to happen at the same time. I love it. Well, thank you so much for being undercover. This has been amazing. Thanks for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
fullText:
Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country.

Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem.

That’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public?

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio.

But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members.

So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view.

Of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the issue.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks for having me, Nilay.

I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation.

I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator company in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks.

What do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans said, “No, we still see through it.”

I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?”

And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.”

You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics.

Is it just that simple?

I hate that it’s that simple.

It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?”

We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it.

It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House.

The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good.

We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work.

So they said, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics.
