The good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the new “gold standard.”

	

Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

Pixel Tag at Amazon

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Google had a privacy focus when launching what was originally called the “Find My Device” network, defaulting the network to only be active on Android phones in “high-traffic areas” only. Users could switch this to “all areas,” but the initial rollout defaulted to effectively cutting off anywhere that wasn’t a major metro, airport/travel hub, etc. It left the network useless to many. Google defended this as a “first-of-its-kind safety protection,” but I’d argue it hindered the network into a state of inefficacy. 

Again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing users to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a new device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone. 

All of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but new hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

fullText:
The Pixel Tag will begin selling in Europe soon, according to a recent leak. The Android Find Hub tracker sold nearly everywhere else during the initial launch.

Google’s very first tracker joined the dozens of other options that work on the Android Find Hub network, launching alongside the Pixel 11 earlier in the year. It’s a sleek little tracking tag, with some first-party care that makes it stand out.

Leaker Roland Quandt posted an update on the Pixel Tag in a recent Bluesky post. It states the Pixel Tag will, in fact, be sold in Europe. There’s no timeline indication in the post, other than a wide-open “pretty soon” tagged on at the end.

 It’s a wonder it didn’t launch in Europe to begin with. Google initially listed 8 countries, including the US, Canada, Australia, India, and Japan. The United Kingdom is included in that list, but the larger portion classified as the European Union is left out.

	

The leak also eases a major concern for users – whether the Pixel Tag will be operational in Europe at all. The Pixel Tag would likely function among the network of Android users in the varying regions, but there’s no definitive answer. But if the Pixel Tag officially lands in Europe, then users won’t need to worry about whether network support will be available.

The Pixel Tag is currently available for nearly every other region online.

title: HomeView missing some podcast feeds? Here’s why
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView features the Podcasts app, but not all feeds appear to be supported for now. Instead, HomeView appears to have the same bug that tvOS 27 introduced to the Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView features the Podcasts app, but not all feeds appear to be supported for now. Instead, HomeView appears to have the same bug that tvOS 27 introduced to the Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

tvOS 27.0 added playback support for HLS-based video podcasts on Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

The same update introduced a bug that dropped support for syncing shows manually added via URL.

Apple’s Podcasts app for iPhone, iPad, and Mac supports adding podcast feeds via URL, a common method for paid subscriber feeds.

The new Apple HomeView appears to have this same bug. Video podcasts using HLS technology are supported, but shows added via URL do not work.

As of tvOS 27.3 beta 1, the bug is still present on Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and newer.

Because tvOS 27 doesn’t run on Apple TV 4K 1st-gen, URL-based subscriptions still work in the Podcasts app — just not HLS-based video feeds.

Anyway, if you’re missing certain feeds in the Podcasts app on HomeView, this is likely the reason.
